note: Scene script for demo/slipday_explainer.mp4 and docs/EXPLAINER.html (final layout, 15 Nov 2026). 'voice' is spoken (synthetic, ElevenLabs); 'caption' is shown under the picture. Every number in either is on screen in that scene.

scenes.title: The question
scenes.caption: A launch can slip by days. Type a site, a date and what the lander needs; Slipday tells you whether the landing still works.
scenes.voice: Rocket launches often slip by a few days. Near the Moon's south pole, that can decide everything. Slipday asks: if the launch slips, can we still land here?

scenes.title: Yes, not sure or no, and the slip margin
scenes.caption: Yes, with 8 days of slip margin. A lander rarely lands exactly on target, so 13 touchdown points within 100 m must all pass.
scenes.voice: The answer is yes, not sure, or no. Here: yes, with eight days of slip margin, checked at thirteen touchdown points around the target.

scenes.title: The challenge objective, in numbers
scenes.caption: The challenge's objective: at touchdown the Sun is 1.2° and the Earth 0.6° above the real skyline. The chart shows their paths.
scenes.voice: This line is the challenge's goal: where the Sun and the Earth stand against the real horizon at touchdown, in numbers, with their paths drawn below.

scenes.title: Launch slipped by N days
scenes.caption: Launch slipped by 9 days: No. Only 95 of the 100 hours of Earth contact; the Earth goes behind ground 131.6 km away.
scenes.voice: Type how many days the launch slipped. Nine days: no. The Earth sinks behind distant ground, so radio contact falls short.

scenes.title: Next windows, other sites, Download
scenes.caption: Miss the window: Dec 17 still works (6 d). In January 13 of 20 other sites work, 11 of them fragile. Download saves the answer.
scenes.voice: Missed the window? December still works. Other sites can work in January, though most are fragile. And one click downloads the whole answer.

scenes.title: The ground in 3-D
scenes.caption: The real ground in 3-D, from the laser altimeter on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA). The shadows move as the Sun circles.
scenes.voice: Here is the real ground in 3-D, from NASA's laser measurements. The low Sun drags long shadows across it.

scenes.title: Your own site
scenes.caption: Type your own spot on the card: 86.000 S, 160.000 W. No: at touchdown the Earth is 4.8° below the skyline.
scenes.voice: You can type your own spot right on the card. Here the answer is no: the Earth is hidden when it lands.

scenes.title: The slip-margin map
scenes.caption: The map colours the ground by days of slip each spot survives: 574 of 733 spots keep a margin at all 13 touchdown points; 159 lose it.
scenes.voice: The map shows how many days of slip each spot survives. Red crosses mark where NASA's finer twenty-metre terrain disagrees.

scenes.title: 80, 20 and 5 m terrain
scenes.caption: Terrain detail matters. At the Shackleton ridge the 80 m map says Yes; the finer 20 m and 5 m maps say Not sure.
scenes.voice: Detail matters. At the Shackleton ridge, the eighty-metre map says yes. The twenty and five-metre maps say not sure.

scenes.title: Is the ground flat enough?
scenes.caption: Flat enough to land? The steepest touchdown point is 4.9°: inside NASA's 8° limit, right at its 5° goal.
scenes.voice: Is the ground flat enough? Here, only just: the steepest spot sits right at NASA's goal for its crewed lander.

scenes.title: Chance of a safe touchdown
scenes.caption: Chance the ground under the lander is within 8°: over 99.9 % for a precision lander, 94 % for a CLPS-class one. Slope only.
scenes.voice: A lander does not come down exactly on target, so this gives the chance the ground under it is flat enough, for three kinds of lander.

scenes.title: A real landing: IM-1
scenes.caption: IM-1 planned about 7 days on the surface. Yes for the February window it flew, and Yes in the January window it missed.
scenes.voice: A real test: the IM-1 lander. The app says yes for the February window it flew, and for the January one it missed.

scenes.title: NASA's nine Artemis regions
scenes.caption: One region is not enough. The best one is open at 28.1% of landing times, three at 40.1%. Sunlight only: 47.8% and 91.1%.
scenes.voice: NASA keeps nine Artemis regions, because one is not enough. The best one is open at twenty-eight point one percent of landing times.

scenes.title: Which years suit a landing
scenes.caption: The same check for every year from 2027 to 2035: the weak season comes a little earlier each year.
scenes.voice: The atlas runs that check for nine years. The weak season comes a little earlier every year.

scenes.title: Relay satellites
scenes.caption: Relay satellites: with two relays of a NASA design (not built yet), contact covers 336 of 336 hours instead of 311 with the Earth alone.
scenes.voice: When the Earth is hidden, a relay satellite circling the Moon could pass messages on. The main answer still counts the Earth alone.

scenes.title: Listen to the landing window
scenes.caption: Listen: the first 14 days as sound. A high tone for the Sun, a low tone for the Earth; it can also be read as text.
scenes.voice: You can also listen to the landing window: a high tone for the Sun, a low one for the Earth, quiet when the ground hides them.

scenes.title: Be the mission planner
scenes.caption: Be the mission planner: the launch slips, you pick one of three sites, and the app shows the real answer for each.
scenes.voice: And a short game for students: the launch slips, you pick a site, and the app shows the real answer.

scenes.title: What it cannot tell you
scenes.caption: Limits: 80 m terrain is coarse and can be too hopeful; the needs are examples; no battery or heat model; fragile answers can flip.
scenes.voice: What it can't tell you: the eighty-metre terrain is coarse and can be too hopeful. The needs are examples, and fragile answers can flip.

scenes.title: Slipday
scenes.caption: Slipday, by [TEAM NAME]. NASA Space Apps 2026: Lunar Landing Site Navigator.
scenes.voice: Slipday. Know your margin before the date moves.
